patterns.title: Inner and Outer Join Filtering
patterns.short_description: Combines rows from two or more tables based on related keys, using WHERE or ON predicates to isolate matched relational entities.
mental_triggers: Combine attributes from multiple related relational tables
Match primary key in one table with foreign key in another
Preserve all rows from left table while filtering right table matches (LEFT JOIN)
constraint_signals: Tables indexed on join keys allow nested loop or hash join in O(M + N)
Missing records should be filled with NULL (requires LEFT JOIN)
patterns.complexity: Query Time: O(M log N) or O(M + N) with index on join key | Space: O(M + N)
patterns.base_template_sql:
SELECT a.id, a.name, b.department_name
FROM Employees a
LEFT JOIN Departments b ON a.department_id = b.id
WHERE b.is_active = 1;
patterns.base_template_py:
import pandas as pd

def join_filter(employees: pd.DataFrame, departments: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    merged = employees.merge(departments, left_on="department_id", right_on="id", how="left")
    return merged[merged["is_active"] == 1][["id", "name", "department_name"]]

patterns.title: Anti-Join (Exclusion Filtering)
patterns.short_description: Identifies rows in a primary table that have no corresponding match in a secondary table using LEFT JOIN with IS NULL, NOT EXISTS, or NOT IN.
mental_triggers: Find customers who never placed an order
Identify entities present in table A but missing in table B
Detect orphaned foreign keys or unused reference entries
constraint_signals: Nullable columns in secondary table can make NOT IN fail; NOT EXISTS or LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL is safer and index-friendly
patterns.complexity: Query Time: O(M + N) with index-backed foreign key | Space: O(M) temporary set
patterns.base_template_sql:
SELECT c.name AS Customers
FROM Customers c
LEFT JOIN Orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.customer_id IS NULL;
patterns.base_template_py:
import pandas as pd

def anti_join(customers: pd.DataFrame, orders: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    active_ids = orders["customer_id"].dropna().unique()
    return customers[~customers["id"].isin(active_ids)][["name"]]

patterns.title: Grouped Aggregation
patterns.short_description: Partitions table rows by one or more dimension columns and computes summary statistics (COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX) per group.
mental_triggers: Calculate total sales per department or user
Find maximum transaction amount per day
Count distinct activities grouped by account status
constraint_signals: High-cardinality grouping requires memory hash table; pre-sorted input or index on GROUP BY keys avoids temporary files
patterns.complexity: Query Time: O(N log N) or O(N) with index grouping | Space: O(K) where K is number of groups

patterns.title: Aggregate Filtering (HAVING)
patterns.short_description: Applies selection criteria to post-aggregation bucket metrics, filtering out aggregated groups that fail threshold conditions.
mental_triggers: Find classes with at least 5 students
Identify users whose total transaction sum exceeds $1,000
Select duplicate emails appearing more than once
constraint_signals: Filter conditions reference aggregate functions (COUNT, SUM, AVG) rather than raw individual row attributes
patterns.complexity: Query Time: O(N log N) for grouping + O(K) bucket filter | Space: O(K) groups
patterns.base_template_sql:
SELECT email
FROM Person
GROUP BY email
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
patterns.base_template_py:
import pandas as pd

def having_filter(person: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    counts = person.groupby("email").size().reset_index(name="cnt")
    return counts[counts["cnt"] > 1][["email"]]

patterns.title: Window Ranking Functions
patterns.short_description: Computes positional ordinal ranks across partitions without collapsing rows, distinguishing between ROW_NUMBER(), RANK(), and DENSE_RANK().
mental_triggers: Find top 3 highest-earning employees in each department
Rank students by test score handling ties without skipping ranks (DENSE_RANK)
Assign sequential IDs to events per session
constraint_signals: Result requires retaining individual row identity while assigning rank values partitioned by department or category
patterns.complexity: Query Time: O(N log N) for window sorting | Space: O(N) window frame buffer
patterns.base_template_sql:
SELECT score, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC) AS 
FROM Scores;

patterns.title: Window Offset Access (LEAD and LAG)
patterns.short_description: Accesses values from preceding (LAG) or subsequent (LEAD) rows within an ordered partition without requiring self-joins.
mental_triggers: Compare current day temperature to previous day
Detect consecutive logons within 5 minutes of previous logon
Calculate day-over-day percentage change in revenue
constraint_signals: Chronological row comparisons where each row must inspect adjacent previous/next row within partition
patterns.complexity: Query Time: O(N log N) for ordered partitioning | Space: O(N) window frame buffer
patterns.base_template_sql:
SELECT DISTINCT num AS ConsecutiveNums
FROM (
    SELECT num,
           LAG(num, 1) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS prev_num,
           LEAD(num, 1) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS next_num
    FROM Logs
) t
WHERE num = prev_num AND num = next_num;

patterns.title: Running Total and Moving Aggregates
patterns.short_description: Computes cumulative sums, moving averages, or bounded range sums over ordered rows using window frames (ROWS BETWEEN).
mental_triggers: Calculate cumulative bank balance across transaction history
Compute 7-day rolling average of daily user signups
Running total of items purchased over time per user
constraint_signals: ORDER BY inside OVER() creates cumulative frame (RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) by default
With ORDER BY, the default frame is RANGE, so tied rows share one running total; use ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW for strict row-by-row totals.
patterns.complexity: Query Time: O(N log N) for sorting | Space: O(N) window buffer

patterns.title: Top N Records per Group
patterns.short_description: Extracts the top or bottom N records within each category or partition using window ranking inside a CTE or derived table.
mental_triggers: Find top 3 highest paid employees in each department
Select most recent 2 orders for each customer
Identify top selling product in each category
constraint_signals: Requires subquery or CTE because window functions cannot appear directly in WHERE clause
patterns.complexity: Query Time: O(N log N) window sort + O(N) outer predicate | Space: O(N) CTE materialization
patterns.base_template_sql:
WITH Ranked AS (
    SELECT e.id, e.name, e.salary, e.departmentId,
           DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY e.departmentId ORDER BY e.salary DESC) AS rnk
    FROM Employee e
)
SELECT d.name AS Department, r.name AS Employee, r.salary AS Salary
FROM Ranked r
JOIN Department d ON r.departmentId = d.id
WHERE r.rnk <= 3;

patterns.title: Self-Join Relationships
patterns.short_description: Joins a table to itself to compare rows within the same dataset, such as manager-employee hierarchies or consecutive date entries.
mental_triggers: Find employees who earn more than their direct manager
Compare records with their own previous date entry without window functions
Graph or tree node relationships stored in a single table
constraint_signals: Single table contains both the entity and a foreign key pointing to another row in the same table
patterns.complexity: Query Time: O(N log N) or O(N^2) unindexed | Space: O(N) intermediate join table
patterns.base_template_sql:
SELECT e.name AS Employee
FROM Employee e
JOIN Employee m ON e.managerId = m.id
WHERE e.salary > m.salary;

patterns.title: Gaps and Islands Detection
patterns.short_description: Groups consecutive sequential rows into contiguous islands or detects missing intervals (gaps) using ROW_NUMBER difference techniques.
mental_triggers: Find users with 3 or more consecutive days of active logins
Identify contiguous date ranges during which a machine was operational
Detect missing invoice numbers in a sequential sequence
constraint_signals: Subtracting ROW_NUMBER() from a date or sequence number yields a constant invariant for all rows in the same contiguous island
patterns.complexity: Query Time: O(N log N) window sort + O(N) group aggregation | Space: O(N) window tracking buffer
patterns.base_template_sql:
WITH Numbered AS (
    SELECT log_date,
           DATE_SUB(log_date, INTERVAL ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY log_date) DAY) AS island_id
    FROM UserActivity
)
SELECT MIN(log_date) AS start_date, MAX(log_date) AS end_date, COUNT(*) AS streak_length
FROM Numbered
GROUP BY island_id;

patterns.title: Recursive Common Table Expressions
patterns.short_description: Iteratively evaluates anchor and recursive member queries to traverse graphs, hierarchies, or generate numerical sequences.
mental_triggers: Traverse multi-level organizational charts (CEO down to entry-level)
Generate a sequence of dates between start_date and end_date
Find all indirect connections or prerequisites in a graph
constraint_signals: Depth of tree or chain is arbitrary and not known at query authoring time; requires termination condition
patterns.complexity: Time: O(rows produced) | Space: O(rows produced) where the engine materializes the CTE

dialect_notes.mysql: cte_max_recursion_depth defaults to 1000, so long sequences such as date ranges need it raised or a different approach.

patterns.base_template_sql:
WITH RECURSIVE Hierarchy AS (
    SELECT id, name, manager_id, 1 AS depth
    FROM Employees
    WHERE manager_id IS NULL
    UNION ALL
    SELECT e.id, e.name, e.manager_id, h.depth + 1
    FROM Employees e
    JOIN Hierarchy h ON e.manager_id = h.id
)
SELECT * FROM Hierarchy ORDER BY depth, id;
patterns.base_template_py:
import pandas as pd

def recursive_hierarchy(employees: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    roots = employees[employees["manager_id"].isna()].copy()
    roots["depth"] = 1
    levels = [roots]
    while True:
        curr = levels[-1]
        nxt = employees.merge(curr[["id", "depth"]], left_on="manager_id", right_on="id", suffixes=("", "_parent"))
        if nxt.empty: break
        nxt["depth"] = nxt["depth"] + 1
        levels.append(nxt[["id", "name", "manager_id", "depth"]])
    return pd.concat(levels, ignore_index=True)

patterns.title: Conditional Aggregation and Pivoting
patterns.short_description: Transforms row-level categorical data into column-level summaries using CASE WHEN expressions nested inside aggregate functions.
mental_triggers: Transpose row-based monthly sales into 12 distinct month columns
Count occurrences of different statuses in separate columns in a single row
Calculate proportion or ratio of specific events to total events
constraint_signals: Input is tall/narrow and target output is wide with fixed column headers for each category value
patterns.complexity: Query Time: O(N) single-pass aggregate over groups | Space: O(K) where K is distinct groups
patterns.base_template_sql:
SELECT product_id,
       SUM(CASE WHEN store = "store1" THEN price ELSE NULL END) AS store1,
       SUM(CASE WHEN store = "store2" THEN price ELSE NULL END) AS store2,
       SUM(CASE WHEN store = "store3" THEN price ELSE NULL END) AS store3
FROM Products
GROUP BY product_id;

patterns.title: Date and Time Arithmetic
patterns.short_description: Performs interval manipulation, boundary extraction, and difference calculations across temporal fields using engine-specific date functions.
mental_triggers: Find records created within the last 30 days
Calculate duration in days or hours between order_date and ship_date
Group transactions by year-month or day of week
constraint_signals: Comparing dates must handle leap years, month boundaries, and timestamp vs date casting (e.g. DATEDIFF)
patterns.complexity: Query Time: O(N) linear evaluation; can use index range scan if function is not wrapped on column | Space: O(1)

dialect_notes.general: Date and interval functions differ significantly across SQL engines (e.g. DATEDIFF in MySQL vs interval arithmetic in PostgreSQL).

patterns.base_template_sql:
SELECT w1.id
FROM Weather w1
JOIN Weather w2 ON DATEDIFF(w1.recordDate, w2.recordDate) = 1
WHERE w1.temperature > w2.temperature;
patterns.base_template_py:
import pandas as pd

def date_time_cmp(weather: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    weather["recordDate"] = pd.to_datetime(weather["recordDate"])
    weather = weather.sort_values("recordDate").reset_index(drop=True)
    date_diff = (weather["recordDate"] - weather["recordDate"].shift(1)).dt.days
    temp_diff = weather["temperature"] - weather["temperature"].shift(1)
    return weather[(date_diff == 1) & (temp_diff > 0)][["id"]]

patterns.title: String Manipulation and Pattern Matching
patterns.short_description: Performs pattern matching, case conversion, token concatenation, and regex validation on text columns.
mental_triggers: Find users with valid email format starting with a letter
Capitalize first character of names and lowercase remaining characters
Group comma-separated lists of products per user (GROUP_CONCAT)
constraint_signals: LIKE wildcards with leading % cannot use B-tree index; regex functions evaluate per row
patterns.complexity: Query Time: O(N * L) where L is string length | Space: O(L) output buffer

patterns.title: Set Operations (UNION, INTERSECT, EXCEPT)
patterns.short_description: Combines or compares row sets from multiple SELECT queries using set union, intersection, or difference semantics.
mental_triggers: Combine customers from active and archived regional databases
Find IDs that appear in both table A and table B (INTERSECT)
Find all items present in catalogue but never appearing in orders (EXCEPT)
constraint_signals: UNION removes duplicates with sorting/hashing; UNION ALL preserves all rows without duplicate removal overhead

patterns.title: NULL Values, COALESCE & Safe Comparison
patterns.short_description: Managing three-valued logic (TRUE, FALSE, UNKNOWN) using COALESCE, IFNULL, IS NULL, and understanding aggregate NULL elimination.
mental_triggers: Customer Placing Largest Number of Orders: replacing NULL totals with 0 via COALESCE
Find Customers With Positive Revenue: filtering where column IS NOT NULL vs > 0
Aggregates ignoring NULL: COUNT(column) counts non-nulls whereas COUNT(*) counts rows
constraint_signals: Arithmetic with NULL produces NULL; comparing with = NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN
patterns.complexity: Query Time: O(N) row evaluation | Space: O(1)
patterns.base_template_sql:
SELECT e.name, b.bonus
FROM Employee e
LEFT JOIN Bonus b ON e.empId = b.empId
WHERE COALESCE(b.bonus, 0) < 1000;
patterns.base_template_py:
import pandas as pd

def null_handling(employee: pd.DataFrame, bonus: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    merged = employee.merge(bonus, on="empId", how="left")
    merged["bonus"] = merged["bonus"].fillna(0)
    return merged[merged["bonus"] < 1000][["name", "bonus"]]

patterns.title: Correlated Subqueries & EXISTS Logic
patterns.short_description: Evaluating subqueries that reference columns from the outer query for each outer row, typically with EXISTS or scalar aggregations.
mental_triggers: Employees Earning More Than Their Department Average: correlated AVG in WHERE clause
Customers Who Bought All Products: NOT EXISTS (NOT EXISTS) relational division
Find Managers with At Least 5 Direct Reports: EXISTS / COUNT in subquery
constraint_signals: Correlated subqueries execute per candidate outer row unless rewritten by query optimizer into a join
patterns.complexity: Query Time: O(M * N) unindexed, O(M log N) with index | Space: O(1)
patterns.base_template_sql:
SELECT e.name
FROM Employee e
WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM Employee sub
    WHERE sub.managerId = e.id
    HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5
);
patterns.base_template_py:
import pandas as pd

def exists_subquery(employee: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    mgr_counts = employee["managerId"].value_counts()
    valid_ids = mgr_counts[mgr_counts >= 5].index
    return employee[employee["id"].isin(valid_ids)][["name"]]

mental_triggers: Second Highest Salary: SELECT DISTINCT salary ... ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1
Nth Highest Salary: encapsulated SQL function taking N and using OFFSET N-1
Returning NULL automatically if Nth highest value does not exist (wrapping in outer SELECT)

Wrapping query in subquery ensures returning NULL instead of an empty result set

patterns.short_description: Modifying database tables in-place using DELETE with self-joins or UPDATE with conditional CASE expressions.

import pandas as pd

hints.text: Nations qualify as large either by territorial expanse exceeding three million or by human population reaching twenty-five million.

hints.title: Disjunctive Filter Predicate
hints.text: Combine the geographic and demographic thresholds in a where clause using the logical or operator.

hints.title: Projection Selection Blueprint
hints.text: Select name, population, area from World where area >= 3000000 or population >= 25000000.

hints.title: Complete Implementation
hints.text:
```mysql
SELECT name, population, area
FROM World
WHERE area >= 3000000 OR population >= 25000000;
```

complexity.whyNaiveFails: Full Cartesian joins or redundant unions add latency over simple single-pass filtering.

import pandas as pd

def big_countries(world: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:

hints.title: Class Enrollment Aggregation
hints.text: The table records student enrollments across distinct courses. How can you group enrollment records by academic course and filter for courses that contain at least five enrolled students?

hints.title: Course Size Invariant
hints.text: Grouping by course name consolidates student enrollments into singular course aggregates whose size can be filtered with a post-aggregation clause.

hints.title: Group By Course Having Procedure
hints.text: Group the Courses records by class name. Filter using a having clause where count of student is at least five, and select the class column.

hints.title: Complete Implementation
hints.text:
```mysql
SELECT class
FROM Courses
GROUP BY class
HAVING COUNT(student) >= 5;
```

complexity.notes: Single pass group by aggregation with having count filter.
complexity.whyNaiveFails: Scanning all student rows repeatedly for each distinct class takes O(C * N) time.
complexity.spaceTimeTradeoff: Group by with having aggregates courses in O(N) time with O(C) memory for course buckets.
complexity.interviewerExpectation: Properly grouping by class; filtering with having count >= 5.

solutions.code:

FROM Courses

HAVING COUNT(student) >= 5;

import pandas as pd

def find_classes(courses: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:

hints.title: Preserving Incomplete Records
hints.text: Each person must appear in the final report even when no matching location data exists in the address table. How can two relational tables be connected without discarding rows that lack a corresponding foreign key match?

hints.title: Outer Join Matching
hints.text: A standard inner join excludes records that fail the match condition. An outer join retains every record from the primary table and supplies null values for unmatched columns.

hints.title: Left Join Specification
hints.text: Execute a left outer join from Person to Address matching on personId. Select firstName and lastName from Person along with city and state from Address. Rows in Person without an Address row will automatically produce null for city and state.

hints.title: Complete Implementation
hints.text:
```mysql
SELECT p.firstName, p.lastName, a.city, a.state
FROM Person p
LEFT JOIN Address a ON p.personId = a.personId;
```

complexity.notes: Single pass outer hash or index join over Person and Address tables.
complexity.whyNaiveFails: A Cartesian product (FROM Person, Address) produces P x A intermediate rows before filtering with a WHERE clause. For large tables, this materializes unnecessary cross-product tuples in memory. An INNER JOIN erroneously discards people who do not have an address entry.
complexity.spaceTimeTradeoff: A LEFT JOIN with index support on Address(personId) streams the outer table in O(P) time with O(1) extra space, or performs a single-pass hash join in O(P + A) time and O(P) auxiliary memory without intermediate sorting.
complexity.interviewerExpectation: Immediate recognition of LEFT JOIN semantics to retain Person rows having null address fields; leveraging foreign key indexes on personId.

solutions.approach: Left Outer Join on Foreign Key
PostgreSQL Left Outer Join on personId

solutions.code:
import pandas as pd

def combine_two_tables(person: pd.DataFrame, address: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    merged = person.merge(address, on='personId', how='left')
    return merged[['firstName', 'lastName', 'city', 'state']]

hints.title: Sequential Row Triplet Matching
hints.text: The table records numbers logged in sequential identifier order. How can you inspect the immediately preceding and succeeding values around each row to identify numbers repeated across at least three continuous occurrences?

hints.title: Window Offset Invariant
hints.text: In an unbroken sequence of three identical numbers ordered by identifier, looking backward one row and forward one row yields the exact same value as the current record.

hints.title: Lead and Lag Filtering Procedure
hints.text: Use window offset functions over sequential identifier order to retrieve the prior value and next value. Wrap in a subquery and select unique numbers where current matches both neighboring values.

hints.title: Complete Implementation
hints.text:
```mysql
SELECT DISTINCT num AS ConsecutiveNums
FROM (
    SELECT num,
           LAG(num, 1) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS prev_num,
           LEAD(num, 1) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS next_num,
           LAG(id, 1) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS prev_id,
           LEAD(id, 1) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS next_id,
           id
    FROM Logs
) t
WHERE num = prev_num AND num = next_num AND prev_id = id - 1 AND next_id = id + 1;
```

variables: N: total records in Logs table
complexity.notes: Window lead and lag offsets over sorted identifier order with distinct result filtering.
complexity.whyNaiveFails: Three-way self-joins (Logs l1 JOIN Logs l2 JOIN Logs l3) assume strictly continuous integer identifiers without gaps and perform quadratic tuple comparisons.
complexity.spaceTimeTradeoff: Window offsets evaluate consecutive rows in O(N log N) sorting time and O(N) memory without Cartesian explosion.
complexity.interviewerExpectation: Handling identifier gaps correctly by sorting or windowing; removing duplicate matches with DISTINCT.

           LEAD(num, 1) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS next_num,
           LAG(id, 1) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS prev_id,
           LEAD(id, 1) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS next_id,
           id
    FROM Logs
) t
WHERE num = prev_num AND num = next_num AND prev_id = id - 1 AND next_id = id + 1;

    FROM Logs

hints.title: Detecting Missing Foreign References
hints.text: Every purchase references a customer identifier in the orders table. How can you inspect all registered users and identify those who have zero corresponding foreign key records in the purchases table?

hints.title: Anti-Join Null Invariant
hints.text: A left outer join retains all primary table records. Rows without a match in the secondary table populate secondary columns with null, allowing an anti-join filter.

hints.title: Left Join Null Filter Procedure
hints.text: Perform a left join from Customers to Orders on customer identifier. In the where clause, filter for records where the joined order identifier is null, and select the customer name.

hints.title: Complete Implementation
hints.text:
```mysql
SELECT c.name AS Customers
FROM Customers c
LEFT JOIN Orders o ON c.id = o.customerId
WHERE o.customerId IS NULL;
```

complexity.notes: Single pass outer hash or index join with null foreign key filter.
complexity.whyNaiveFails: Using NOT IN with a subquery fails catastrophically or produces null if any order customerId contains a NULL value in SQL.
complexity.spaceTimeTradeoff: A left outer join with IS NULL filter streams in O(C + O_cnt) time and requires O(C) memory for hash matching.
complexity.interviewerExpectation: Knowing the pitfall of NOT IN with NULLs; preferring LEFT JOIN / IS NULL or NOT EXISTS for robustness.

SELECT c.name AS Customers
FROM Customers c
LEFT JOIN Orders o ON c.id = o.customerId
WHERE o.customerId IS NULL;

hints.title: In-Place Row Removal
hints.text: The objective is modifying table contents directly rather than generating a filtered report. When identical values appear across multiple rows, how can rows with higher identifiers be identified for deletion?

hints.title: Self-Join Comparison
hints.text: Joining a table to itself on matching values allows direct comparison between distinct rows sharing the same attribute. Identifying duplicate pairs enables targeting rows with greater identifiers.

hints.title: Targeted Join Deletion
hints.text: Construct a delete statement referencing the first table instance while joining it to a second instance of Person on equal email addresses and the condition that the first row id is greater than the second row id. This deletes only redundant rows with higher IDs.

hints.title: Complete Implementation
hints.text:
```mysql
DELETE p1
FROM Person p1
JOIN Person p2 ON p1.email = p2.email AND p1.id > p2.id;
```

complexity.notes: Multi-table DELETE self-join matching email with greater id.
complexity.whyNaiveFails: A naive DELETE FROM Person WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT MIN(id) FROM Person GROUP BY email) in MySQL fails with error 1093 ("You cannot specify target table for update in FROM clause"). A naive subquery also risks full-table locking.
complexity.spaceTimeTradeoff: Self-joining Person p1 JOIN Person p2 on matching email and p1.id > p2.id allows MySQL and PostgreSQL to delete in-place during the join scan in O(N log N) time without temporary materialized subquery tables.
complexity.interviewerExpectation: Understanding MySQL multi-table DELETE syntax (DELETE p1 FROM Person p1 JOIN Person p2); ensuring that only duplicate rows with strictly larger IDs are deleted while retaining the minimal ID.

solutions.code:
import pandas as pd

# Modify Person in place
def delete_duplicate_emails(person: pd.DataFrame) -> None:
    person.sort_values(by='id', ascending=True, inplace=True)
    null_rows = person[person['email'].isna()]
    valid_rows = person[person['email'].notna()].drop_duplicates(subset=['email'], keep='first')
    combined = pd.concat([valid_rows, null_rows]).sort_values(by='id')
    person.drop(person.index.difference(combined.index), inplace=True)
solutions.approach: Pandas In-Place Sort and Drop Duplicates

hints.title: Grouped Extremum Matching
hints.text: Each department can contain multiple individuals sharing the maximum compensation value. How can employees be filtered by matching both their department association and their compensation against calculated maximums?

hints.title: Composite In-Filter on Aggregates
hints.text: Grouping records by department determines the peak compensation for each unit. Filtering the base table using a composite tuple match on department identifier and compensation keeps all top earners.

hints.title: Group Subquery with Department Join
hints.text: Compute the maximum salary per department using a grouped subquery on departmentId. Join Employee with Department, and filter records where the tuple of departmentId and salary matches the subquery results. Select the department name, employee name, and salary.

hints.title: Complete Implementation
hints.text:
```mysql
SELECT d.name AS Department, e.name AS Employee, e.salary AS Salary
FROM Employee e
JOIN Department d ON e.departmentId = d.id
WHERE (e.departmentId, e.salary) IN (
  SELECT departmentId, MAX(salary)
  FROM Employee
  GROUP BY departmentId
);
```

complexity.notes: Inner join with grouped maximum salary subquery on (departmentId, salary).
complexity.whyNaiveFails: Correlated subqueries in the SELECT clause (SELECT (SELECT MAX(...) ... WHERE ...)) execute once per employee row (O(E * E) full scans). Joining without a composite tuple match (departmentId, salary) can mismatch salaries across different departments.
complexity.spaceTimeTradeoff: Grouping once by department to compute MAX(salary) requires O(E) time and O(D) hash table memory, enabling an optimal hash-semijoin in O(E + D) total execution time.
complexity.interviewerExpectation: Handling salary ties properly (if two employees in the same department share the max salary, both must be returned); using composite tuple matching or window functions (DENSE_RANK()).

hints.title: Partitioned Multi-Level High Earners
hints.text: Each organizational division has multiple earners and potentially tied salaries. How can you rank compensation independently within each division so that up to three distinct top amounts are included?

hints.title: Partitioned Dense Rank Invariant
hints.text: Dense ranking partitioned by department identifier orders salaries within each group independently, ensuring tied earners share rank without consuming subsequent rank slots.

hints.title: Partitioned Window Join Procedure
hints.text: In a subquery, compute dense rank partitioned by department identifier ordered by salary descending. Join with Department on department identifier and filter where rank is at most three.

hints.title: Complete Implementation
hints.text:
```mysql
SELECT d.name AS Department, e.name AS Employee, e.salary AS Salary
FROM (
    SELECT name, salary, departmentId,
           DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY departmentId ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk
    FROM Employee
) e
JOIN Department d ON e.departmentId = d.id
WHERE e.rnk <= 3;
```

variables: N: total employees across all departments
complexity.notes: Partitioned window dense rank with inner join to Department table.
complexity.whyNaiveFails: Correlated self-joins counting distinct higher salaries take O(N^2) time, which times out on departments with thousands of employees.
complexity.spaceTimeTradeoff: Window partitioning sorts each department group in O(N log N) overall time and O(N) memory.
complexity.interviewerExpectation: Using DENSE_RANK() with PARTITION BY; joining with department table to present department name.

hints.title: Left Outer Join and Null Checking

import pandas as pd

def employee_bonus(employee: pd.DataFrame, bonus: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    merged = employee.merge(bonus, on='empId', how='left')
    filtered = merged[(merged['bonus'] < 1000) | (merged['bonus'].isna())]
    return filtered[['name', 'bonus']]

hints.title: Consecutive Day Threshold Island Detection
hints.text: Peak attendance records must span three or more contiguous calendar identifiers where headcount reaches or exceeds one hundred.

hints.title: Contiguity Grouping via Row Number Offset
hints.text: Filter entries with people >= 100. Subtract row_number() over (order by id) from id to assign contiguous sequences to an identical grouping key.

hints.title: Common Table Expression Island Blueprint
hints.text: Construct a CTE with id - row_number() over (order by id) as grp. Join with a subquery filtering for group sizes >= 3, and order by id.

hints.title: Complete Implementation
hints.text:
```mysql
WITH HighTraffic AS (
    SELECT id, visit_date, people,
           id - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY id) AS grp
    FROM Stadium
    WHERE people >= 100
),
GroupCounts AS (
    SELECT grp, COUNT(*) AS cnt
    FROM HighTraffic
    GROUP BY grp
    HAVING cnt >= 3
)
SELECT h.id, h.visit_date, h.people
FROM HighTraffic h
JOIN GroupCounts g ON h.grp = g.grp
ORDER BY h.id;
```

complexity.notes: Window function row number assignment followed by group size filtering.
complexity.whyNaiveFails: Three-way self-joins take cubic O(S^3) time without indexes and miss islands longer than 3 days without duplicate handling.
complexity.spaceTimeTradeoff: Gaps-and-islands window grouping isolates contiguous runs in a single sorting pass.
complexity.interviewerExpectation: Proficiency with gaps-and-islands logic using ROW_NUMBER() difference technique.

hints.title: Temporal Sequence Comparison
hints.text: Comparing an entry against its immediate predecessor cannot rely solely on sequential identifiers, because dates may contain gaps. How can records be matched precisely to the calendar day preceding them?

hints.title: Date Arithmetic Self-Join
hints.text: Joining the table with itself using date arithmetic allows linking each measurement directly to the entry from exactly one day earlier. Temperature values can then be compared across the paired records.

hints.title: One-Day Offset Matching
hints.text: Join Weather w1 with Weather w2 where w1.recordDate equals the date one day after w2.recordDate. Add a filter requiring w1.temperature to be strictly greater than w2.temperature, and project w1.id.

hints.title: Complete Implementation
hints.text:
```mysql
SELECT w1.id
FROM Weather w1
JOIN Weather w2 ON w1.recordDate = DATE_ADD(w2.recordDate, INTERVAL 1 DAY)
WHERE w1.temperature > w2.temperature;
```

complexity.notes: Self-join matching recordDate with yesterday using DATE_ADD interval.
complexity.whyNaiveFails: A cross-join of Weather with itself without indexed date arithmetic scans N^2 pairs. Filtering by w1.id = w2.id + 1 fails when record IDs are non-consecutive or dates have gaps; date differences must be measured using temporal intervals.
complexity.spaceTimeTradeoff: Self-joining on w1.recordDate = DATE_ADD(w2.recordDate, INTERVAL 1 DAY) utilizes a B-tree index on recordDate, reducing execution from quadratic nested scans to O(N) index-lookup time with O(1) temporary memory.
complexity.interviewerExpectation: Using date arithmetic functions (DATE_ADD in MySQL, + INTERVAL '1 day' in PostgreSQL) rather than subtracting IDs; strictly comparing temperatures with >.

solutions.code:
SELECT w1.id
FROM Weather w1
JOIN Weather w2 ON w1.recordDate = DATE_ADD(w2.recordDate, INTERVAL 1 DAY)
WHERE w1.temperature > w2.temperature;

FROM Weather w1
JOIN Weather w2 ON w1.recordDate = w2.recordDate + INTERVAL '1 day'
WHERE w1.temperature > w2.temperature;

import pandas as pd

def rising_temperature(weather: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    weather['recordDate'] = pd.to_datetime(weather['recordDate'])
    weather = weather.sort_values('recordDate')
    prev_weather = weather.copy()
    prev_weather['recordDate'] = prev_weather['recordDate'] + pd.Timedelta(days=1)
    merged = weather.merge(prev_weather, on='recordDate', suffixes=('', '_prev'))
    rising = merged[merged['temperature'] > merged['temperature_prev']]
    return rising[['id']]

import pandas as pd

def sales_person(sales_person: pd.DataFrame, company: pd.DataFrame, orders: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    red_companies = company[company['name'] == 'RED']['com_id']
    red_sales_ids = orders[orders['com_id'].isin(red_companies)]['sales_id'].unique()
    result = sales_person[~sales_person['sales_id'].isin(red_sales_ids)]
    return result[['name']]

hints.title: Missing Value Handling
hints.text: Finding the second distinct value requires skipping ties and the maximum value. What query structure guarantees that an empty result set converts cleanly into a single row containing a null value?

hints.title: Distinct Paging and Scalar Subquery
hints.text: Deduplicating entries before ranking ensures identical amounts do not occupy multiple positions. Wrapping the selected value in a scalar subquery converts an empty row count into a null result.

hints.title: Offset Selection with Subquery Fallback

FROM Triangle;

import pandas as pd

def triangle_judgement(triangle: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    cond = (triangle['x'] + triangle['y'] > triangle['z']) & \
           (triangle['x'] + triangle['z'] > triangle['y']) & \
           (triangle['y'] + triangle['z'] > triangle['x'])
    triangle['triangle'] = cond.map({True: 'Yes', False: 'No'})
    return triangle

hints.text: Requests should only count toward the cancellation metric if neither the customer nor the driver has an active ban status during the measurement period.

hints.title: Dual Table Joins on Role Participants
hints.text: Join the trips table twice against users: once on client identifier and once on driver identifier, asserting that both participants have banned status set to No.

hints.title: Grouped Ratio and Date Restriction
hints.text: Filter for dates between 2013-10-01 and 2013-10-03. Group by request date. Compute the ratio of non-completed trips over total requests using sum and round to two decimal places.

hints.title: Complete Implementation
hints.text:
```mysql
SELECT request_at AS Day,
       ROUND(SUM(status != 'completed') / COUNT(*), 2) AS `Cancellation Rate`
FROM Trips t
JOIN Users c ON t.client_id = c.users_id AND c.banned = 'No'
JOIN Users d ON t.driver_id = d.users_id AND d.banned = 'No'
WHERE request_at BETWEEN '2013-10-01' AND '2013-10-03'
GROUP BY request_at;
```

complexity.spaceTimeTradeoff: Dual inner joins with index lookups on users_id evaluate in linear time with minimal group aggregation memory.
complexity.interviewerExpectation: Ensuring both client and driver unbanned conditions are enforced and rounding ratios to exactly 2 decimals.
